common_name: Marliacea Rosea Water Lily (Classic Pink Hardy Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in aquatic containers of heavy garden loam topped with pea gravel, then lower into 12-24 inches of water once it has warmed in late spring.

directions: Introduced by the Latour-Marliac nursery in 1879, this heirloom hardy water lily opens pale pink flowers that deepen in color with age and cooler weather, held just above rounded, purple-flecked young pads that mature to solid green. It is one of the most vigorous and reliable hardy water lilies ever bred, tolerating a wide range of climates from cold northern ponds to warm southern water gardens without special winter protection where the rhizome sits below the ice line. Plant divisions in heavy, un-amended garden loam topped with pea gravel to keep fish from disturbing the soil, and site in full sun for the heaviest bloom. Established plants spread steadily and benefit from division every three to four years to prevent overcrowding of the pot.

common_name: Rose Arey Water Lily (Fragrant Star-Shaped Pink Hardy Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in aquatic containers of heavy garden loam topped with pea gravel, then lower into 12-24 inches of water once it has warmed in late spring.

directions: Bred by William Tricker and introduced in 1913, Rose Arey produces narrow, star-shaped, richly fragrant pink petals that curve slightly outward, giving each bloom a spidery, delicate look distinct from the rounder flowers of most hardy water lilies. It is a strong, floriferous grower that flowers heavily through summer and holds its color well even as blooms age. Plant divisions in heavy garden loam topped with gravel and place in full sun in 12 to 24 inches of still water for the best flowering. Divide congested tubers every few years in spring as new growth begins to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Sioux Water Lily (Changeable Yellow-to-Red Hardy Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in aquatic containers of heavy garden loam topped with pea gravel, then lower into 12-24 inches of water once it has warmed in late spring.

directions: A Marliac-era changeable hardy water lily dating to the early 1900s, Sioux opens soft apricot-yellow and shifts through orange to a deeper coppery red as each flower ages over several days, so a single plant in bloom can display multiple colors at once. Foliage emerges purple-mottled before maturing to green, adding interest even between flushes of bloom. Plant in heavy loam topped with gravel in a container set in 12 to 24 inches of still water in full sun for the strongest color changes and most prolific flowering. It is a moderate-sized, well-mannered grower suited to small to medium garden ponds.

common_name: Shiroman Lotus (Heirloom Double White Japanese Lotus)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally just under the soil surface in a wide, un-amended clay-loam container once water has warmed, in at least 6-12 inches of standing water over the pot.

directions: A classic Japanese heirloom lotus prized for its huge, fully double, pure white blooms that can reach nearly a foot across, opening over several days with a sweet fragrance before shattering. Its large blue-green leaves rise well above the water on stout stems, giving strong architectural presence in a sizable pond or half-barrel water garden. Plant tubers carefully by hand, since the growing tip snaps easily, in heavy clay-loam topped with a thin layer of gravel to keep fish from uprooting it, then flood gradually as new leaves emerge. Divide only when the container is fully packed with tubers, typically every two to three years, since lotus resents disturbance and may skip a season of bloom after being moved.

common_name: White Japanese Water Iris (Alba Rabbit-Ear Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in heavy, fertile soil in a marginal aquatic container set in 1-4 inches of standing water over the crown, in full sun to light shade.

directions: This white-flowered form of the Japanese water iris bears pure white, three-petaled blooms with a flash of yellow at the throat, held above narrow, upright, sword-like foliage in early summer. Unlike bearded iris, it thrives with its roots permanently submerged in shallow water and performs best planted directly in a marginal pond shelf or a heavy-soil aquatic container. Give it full sun for the strongest bloom, though it tolerates light shade, and avoid limy water or soil, since it prefers a slightly acidic, mineral-poor environment closer to its native bog habitat. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: American Sweet Flag (Native Fertile Sweet Flag)

planting.note: Plant divisions in wet, humus-rich soil at a pond margin or in a marginal aquatic container in 0-4 inches of standing water, in full sun to partial shade.

directions: American sweet flag is the native North American counterpart to the widely planted Eurasian Acorus calamus, distinguished botanically by fewer leaf veins and, unlike the sterile Eurasian triploid, by producing viable seed. It forms upright, iris-like fans of aromatic, sword-shaped leaves along pond edges, marshes, and slow streams, spreading gradually by rhizome into a loose colony useful for erosion control on wet banks. Plant in consistently wet to saturated soil at the water's edge or in a marginal aquatic pot, and give it full sun to partial shade for the best growth. It requires no special winter care in cold climates, dying back to the rhizome and returning reliably each spring.
